overview: “Suren Kingdom” is an uncertain atlas label best explained through Indo-Parthian rulers such as Gondophares. Their connection to Iran’s Suren family is a scholarly hypothesis. The imported span, 1 BCE to 500 CE, greatly exceeds their main period of power. Its broad Sistan-to-Punjab outline repeats across changing regimes, with a mapping gap from 100 to 200. It must not imply one uninterrupted kingdom or unchanged borders. The examples below identify their own dates and places.

periods.title: Early Indo-Parthian power
periods.summary: Regional rulers connected eastern Iran with the northwestern subcontinent before Kushan expansion.

periods.title: Different regional transitions
periods.summary: Western territories entered the early Sasanian political order; the change was not simultaneous everywhere.

periods.title: The atlas continues the label
periods.summary: These later map snapshots cannot establish the survival of an independent Indo-Parthian kingdom.

sections.title: Rulers, money and a complicated name

items.text: Coins reveal regional differences within Indo-Parthian power. In Sistan and near Herat, silver drachms followed Parthian designs and weighed about 3.7 grams. Arachosian bronze coins instead used Greek on one side and Kharoshthi writing on the other. There was no single visual language for every market.

A British Museum coin attributed to Gondophares, dated approximately 32 to 60 CE, shows the king’s diademed head and Nike, the Greek figure of Victory, holding a diadem. Its two scripts and familiar victory imagery show how a new ruler could use older artistic traditions to present his authority.

The Takht-i-Bahi inscription is dated twice: to a ruler’s twenty-sixth year and to year 103 of an era whose identification remains debated. This is why different books can offer different modern dates. The stone survives in Lahore Museum, where it is catalogued as I.1.

sections.title: Courtyards, farming and the problem of rubbish

items.text: House 1E in the excavated Parthian city at Sirkap had more than sixty rooms and four courtyards. A double row of fourteen rooms stood at the front. This substantial complex shows how rooms and open spaces were organized, but it is no blueprint for every family’s home.

Many Sirkap courtyards had no direct doorway from the street, unlike those of the older city at Bhir Mound. Some houses included a small courtyard with a stupa. Routes through a home could therefore separate the street from inner spaces and make room for religious practice.

Taxila’s farmland benefited from rainfall, the Haro River and its tributaries, and springs near the Margala hills. The more fertile northern part of the valley contrasted with stony and scrub-covered areas nearby. Feeding an urban population depended on this local landscape as well as long-distance commerce.

What about rubbish and sewage? Archaeologists found soak-wells and public refuse bins at older Bhir Mound, but the compared Sirkap excavations did not reveal the same arrangements. We cannot simply transfer its predecessor’s plumbing to the Indo-Parthian city, or conclude that no waste disposal existed.

A clay humped bull from Sirkap had a hole through its lower body for an axle, identifying it as a wheeled toy. The excavator assigned it to the second half of the first century CE, across a time of changing rulers. This bull could roll instead of grazing.

Sirkap’s first-half-of-the-first-century deposits yielded an etched carnelian bead, SKR 62. The report also lists shell, glass and terracotta ornaments from other layers. Small personal decorations preserve evidence of craftsmanship and taste alongside the much louder monuments of kings.

A small molded water bottle from the 1944 to 1945 excavations carried rows of cowrie-shell patterns, birds, arches and triangles. Its decoration made an everyday container worth looking at. The report’s vessel collection spans several occupation phases, so this bottle is not assigned to a particular king.

sections.title: Families, healing and a written voice

items.text: The donation inscription associated with Takht-i-Bahi names Balasami together with his son and daughter and honors his mother and father. In Konow’s translation, the gift is a chapel. Three generations enter the record through one religious act, although the monument’s precise original setting and calendar date are not completely secure.

Five metal spatulas from Sirkap were catalogued as surgical instruments, from layers assigned to the first or second century CE. Two surviving examples have flat oval blades. A medical historian compared them with Roman instruments but acknowledged possible religious uses. They are clues to care or ritual, not a confirmed doctor’s kit.

A short Gāndhārī phrase in the stone inscription reads “maharayasa Guduvharasa”, meaning “of the great king Guduvhara.” This is scholarly Roman transliteration of Kharoshthi script, not the original letter shapes. Guduvhara is associated with the name Gondophares; which ruler bore it remains disputed. The inscription belongs broadly to the first century CE, rather than proving the atlas’s full five-century span.

sections.title: How the story was recovered, and what changed

items.text: In 1944, archaeological students trained at Taxila while a smaller trench at Sirkap investigated its layers. A. Ghosh published the results with separate groups for successive building phases. Recording where a bead or toy lay is what allows it to become dated evidence rather than simply an attractive antique.

In the western territories, an inscription of Shapur I names a king of Sakastan among those who served Ardashir I. This places the region within the early Sasanian order in the third century. Local rulers could retain privileges under a new superior, so political transformation did not always mean replacing every institution overnight.

ending.text: Kushan expansion curtailed Indo-Parthian power in the northwest during the first century CE; western territories later entered the Sasanian order. These were different regional changes, not a single fall in 500. Cities, households and religious communities continued under changing rulers.
